input.command:
gh issue comment 298 --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Research complete: recommendation is **no framework integrations**

Write-up lands in #311 as `docs/research/CONSTRAINT_AWARE_ORCHESTRATION_SYNTHESIS.md`. Summary below.

### The finding that reshapes the ticket: archy already ships the contract

Question 3 (advisory vs hard-fail semantics) turned out to be answered by shipped code. `mcp.py:1129`:

```python
sdp_fails_gate = bool(sdp_violations) and config.sdp.mode == "error"
passed = not violations and not sdp_fails_gate
```

`sdp.mode: warn|error` in `archy.yaml` **is** the article's first bullet ("which project rules are advisory and which are hard failures"), decided in config by whoever owns the codebase rather than by the runtime. `sdp_violations` stays populated in warn mode, so all three implied dispositions (block / feed back / annotate) are derivable from one payload today. `Violation` carries `rule`/`source`/`target`/`lines`, enough for a caller to write precise retry feedback. It had simply never been documented as the answer to this question.

### Question 1: the surfaces map, and none of them need archy code

| Framework | Extension point | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| LangChain / LangGraph | `create_agent(middleware=[...])` `after_model` hook (or a node + conditional edge in raw LangGraph) | full control: mutate state, inject a message, `jump_to` |
| Pydantic AI | `@agent.output_validator` | `raise ModelRetry(...)` feeds back and consumes output retry budget. Closest fit. |
| CrewAI | `Task(guardrails=[fn], guardrail_max_retries=N)` | `(False, "msg")` becomes the retry feedback |
| OpenAI Agents SDK | `@output_guardrail` tripwire | hard stop only; caller builds any retry loop |

Each is 10-30 lines: run `archy check`, read `passed`, format violations on failure.

### Question 2: wontfix on native adapters

All four are **already MCP clients** (`langchain-mcp-adapters`, Pydantic AI `MCPToolset`, CrewAI `mcps=[...]`, Agents SDK `MCPServerStdio`/`HostedMCPTool`), so `archy mcp` reaches them today with zero archy code. The tool-access half of "integration" is done.

The real gap is narrow and worth naming: **MCP gives the model the *option* to call archy; a guard runs archy whether the model wants to or not.** The article's fifth bullet is specifically that deterministic path, and MCP by construction cannot express it (no post-generation hook). But that gap is filled by the glue above, not by a package. Four packages, four release cadences, four dependency matrices, tracking four APIs that move fast (LangChain rewrote its agent abstraction into middleware well inside the last year), to wrap a subprocess call and a JSON parse. **Fails the value test.**

### Question 4: the bench is rejected as tautological

A loop that blocks until `archy check` passes produces artifacts that pass `archy check` **by construction**. Measuring "the gate enforced the thing the gate checks" is theater by the definition this repo already uses, and #289/#294 spent a full arm-C harness plus 44 live runs to avoid exactly that trap and come back with a documented null.

The only non-trivial version, recorded in §5 so the design is not lost: **held-out constraints.** Gate on rule set A, never check set B during the run, evaluate B at the end. That tests whether structural feedback makes the agent *globally* more constraint-careful or just A-compliant, and it can genuinely return a null. Substantial bench, no downstream feature riding on the answer. **Not scheduled.**

### Question 5: white paper

Applications *subsection*, not a separate RFC. One paragraph plus one code block: `sdp.mode` as a worked example of the advisory/hard-failure bullet, and `archy check`'s `passed` / exit-code contract as a verifier that drops into any of the four guard hooks. There is no integration to specify, so there is nothing for an RFC to hold.

### The usage-signal gate: zero

`ADOPTERS.md` is empty and every issue in this repo is maintainer-authored. Nobody has asked for LangGraph, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Agents SDK, or anything adjacent. Entirely paper-motivated, which is precisely the case this ticket's second gate was written to catch. Combined with the §4 finding, an integration would be building a distribution channel for a capability nobody has yet asked to reach. Same discipline that deferred the MCP `archy_render` tool in `SPEC_VISUALIZATION.md` §6.3.

### Disposition

| Item | Call |
|---|---|
| Native adapter packages | **Wontfix** |
| Docs recipe page | **Deferred behind a usage signal.** If it lands: one framework tested properly (Pydantic AI), not four rotting snippets against four moving APIs. |
| Gate prototype + bench | **Do not run as specified.** Held-out design recorded, not scheduled. |
| White paper | Short applications subsection |
| Per-rule severity | Filed #309 |
| Canned remediation string | Filed #310 |

Both spinoffs are archy-side and justified independently of any framework: #309 generalizes the dial `sdp.mode` already proves out (a project migrating onto layer rules currently has to choose between deleting a rule and blocking CI), and #310 collapses four hand-rolled renderings of the same violation into one shared renderer, with #145 as a consumer.

Closing as researched. The write-up merges via #311.
EOF
)" && gh issue close 298 --reason completed && echo CLOSED

- **v0.41.0 LIVE on PyPI** (released 2026-07-17). Claude plugin bumped to 0.3.0. Plugin pin `archy>=0.36,<1.0`.
- **11 MCP tools** after **consolidation pass v2 (#265) COMPLETE**: `archy_score`, `archy_cycles`, `archy_check`, `archy_impact`, `archy_snapshot`, `archy_diff`, `archy_simulate`, `archy_graph`, `archy_what_to_refactor_next`, `archy_dsm`, `archy_duplicates`. ## Durable conventions

- **Release rule:** cut a release only on a user-visible `src/archy/` change. bench/tests/docs/plugin-only changes do NOT trigger a release.
- **Plugin pin bump** only on a BC MCP change or a new tool; additive params/fields don't bump it.
- **PyPI publish** has an env gate; I approve it via API when a release was actually requested ([[feedback_pypi_gate_approval]]).
- **Always review via DeepWork** (incl. adversarial), never the code-review skill ([[feedback_use_deepwork_review]]). `.deepreview` is local-only/gitignored ([[feedback_deepreview_local_only]]).
- **Value objects = frozen pydantic** (`class X(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)`), NOT `NamedTuple`/`@dataclass` (22 BaseModel value objects in src/archy). **ONE documented exception: `coupling.CoChangeData` stays a NamedTuple** - hot path, `pair_support` holds millions of dict entries on large repos, never serialized, so pydantic per-item validation is pure cost. Do NOT let a review re-flag it. The DeepWork `python_code_review` rule enforces this; when it flags a NamedTuple, convert unless it's the CoChangeData-shaped case (huge + hot + never-serialized). Migrating: swap `_asdict()`->`model_dump()`, keep computed values as plain `@property` (so `model_dump()` excludes them, matching `_asdict()`).
- **Dogfood archy on itself** as the dev loop ([[feedback_dogfood_archy]]); overall score baseline ~0.67.

## Durable research findings (duplicate detection)

- **~50% precision is the syntactic CEILING**, not a bug: up to ~71% of real clones are benign (Kapser & Godfrey); no production tool solves benign-vs-refactorable syntactically (the boundary is semantic).
- **Co-change is the precision lever** (>94% in the literature): a cluster whose members co-change is refactorable; one that never co-changes is benign. Shipped as `demote_independent` (#242).
- **Exact AST-shape hashing is Type-1/2 only** and misses Type-3 (gapped) clones, the plurality of real clones. Fixed by the token-multiset overlap primitive (#246, opt-in).
- Precision varies by domain: ORM/SDK ~80%, scientific/ML ~33% (mostly test-code + vendored dup) -> path-scoping demotes test/vendored (#247).

## 2026-07-06: cleanliness-paper research -> tickets #259-#262 (all claims adversarially fact-checked first)

**User asked to research arXiv 2605.20049v1 "Does Code Cleanliness Affect Coding Agents? A Controlled Minimal-Pair Study" (SonarSource; HN 48798815), apply to archy, validate every point before filing tickets.** Ran 5 parallel adversarial validation agents against the primary source + web.

**Paper's verified findings:** pass rate FLAT (0.913 clean vs 0.921 messy, -0.9pp) - cleanliness does NOT change task success; footprint shrinks on clean side: input tokens -7.1%, output -8.5%, reasoning chars -11.1%, messages -7.0%; **file revisitation -34% aggregate** (largest effect; "~a third", NOT "halved" - halved is multi-module-track-only). Effect concentrates on MULTI-MODULE tasks. Mechanism = grep-targetability. Config: Sonnet 4.6 / Claude Code, Python+Java only.

**Corrections baked into the tickets (guard against overclaiming):** (1) "module-dependency tooling targets the effect layer" is MY INFERENCE, not a paper finding (paper's lever was SonarQube LINE-level rules; only the TASKS are cross-module). (2) god-object-split "worse" is PER-TASK (Case 2 +8% input tokens), NEUTRAL at track level (+0.1%). (3) TOKENS not dollars (§6: nonlinear). (4) "Opus 4.6 built the variants" is an HN comment (id 48800911), NOT the paper - paper never names the construction model. (5) "duplication misleads agent grep" is practitioner anecdote (HN 48800345/48800118) + indirect academic (arXiv 2510.13859); NO controlled study isolates duplication; do NOT cite 2605.20049 for it. Agent-cost-as-eval-axis prior art = SWE-Effi arXiv 2509.09853.

**#259 is the recommended flagship:** produces archy's own controlled number (apply top recommendation, measure agent token footprint + revisitation before/after, with the unrelated-test-regression gate the paper lacks). New bench category - current bench/ measures architecture metrics, not agent tokens.

## 2026-07-21: #289 stencil 'prewalk' read-reduction -> arm-C bench -> documented NON-RESULT

**Question (#289):** can an archy structural pre-edit brief reduce the exploratory reads a coding agent does before its first edit? (stencil.so/blog/prewalk: the agent bill is O(reads), not O(edits); prewalk's actual win is a warm-*trajectory* handoff, which a tool artifact CANNOT replicate - archy is weak for that; its only shot is (A) substitution, which it already half-ships via `invariant_brief`/`impact`/`graph(focus)` but never measured.)

**Built + ran it.** Added **arm C (context-injection)** to the #259 harness (PR **#294**, branch `alee/armc-read-reduction-289`): inject a 581-tok archy brief into the prompt, measure reads-before-first-edit. New harness code = `pre_edit_reads`/`pre_edit_distinct_files`/`pre_edit_input_tokens`/`made_edit` on the parser, `run_variant(prompt_prefix=)`, `run_arm_c`, A-vs-C `summarize`, `--mode ac`. Config: flask @ 36e4a82, `claude-sonnet-5`, teardown-ordering task (true surface 3 files: sansio/app.py + app.py + ctx.py), brief precision 0.33 (named 9 files, 3 on-surface).

**Result = NON-RESULT.** Pooled **N=22** (a stalled headless claude at run 22 killed, unpaired arm dropped): `pre_edit_reads` median delta **-2.0, 14/8 pairs, sign p=0.286**. An N=10 hint (median -3.5, p=0.109) **did NOT survive doubling N**. `pre_edit_distinct_files` UNCHANGED (delta=0) - the agent found the ~3-file spine unaided, so **no headroom for any brief on an easy/grep-able task**. `num_turns` nominally -5 (p=0.041) but FAILS multiple-comparison correction and is not a read count (do NOT relabel as read reduction). 0 regressions throughout. **NO-GO on an `archy brief` feature, on EVIDENCE** (effect regressed to null on more data) - the anti-theater gate working: the N=10 hint would've shipped theater.

**Durable lesson:** briefs help where an agent WOULD flounder (large/unfamiliar repo, non-grep-discoverable surface, weak/cheap executor a-la prewalk's frontier->cheap), NOT on easy tasks where it finds the spine itself. The path to a significant brief effect is a harder *setting*, not a better *brief* (breadth was flat even with the noisy brief, so lifting brief precision has a weak prior). A small true effect won't clear significance at N~22 anyway (needs N~50-100 or a bigger effect). Findings note `docs/research/PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md` (§6 result, §7 headroom-scoping); result table in `bench/agent_footprint_results.md`.

**Tickets (all CLOSED 2026-07-21):** #289 research (findings note merged PR #294); #290 brief precision metric, #291 task-conditioned focus, #293 metric split - all CLOSED as mooted by the non-result (contingent on the brief helping, which it did not; reopen only for a harder-setting rerun per §7); #292 power-to-N30 CLOSED (answered by the N=22 null); #295 pydantic migration DONE (PR #296). **Net: the whole #289 arc is closed - a documented non-result, no feature, nothing left open.** Reopen path if ever revisited: a HARDER setting (unfamiliar/large repo, non-grep surface, weak/cheap executor), NOT a better brief.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/hosanglee/.claude/plugins/cache/deepwork-plugins/deepwork/0.14.0/skills/review

# DeepWork Review

Run automated code reviews on the current branch based on `.deepreview` config files.

## Routing — Check Before Proceeding

**STOP and redirect** if either of these applies:

- User wants to **configure, create, or modify** review rules (e.g., "add a security review", "set up reviews for our API layer") → use the `configure_reviews` skill instead
- User wants to **add a doc-sync rule** (keep a documentation file in sync with source files) → call `start_workflow` with `job_name="deepwork_reviews"` and `workflow_name="add_document_update_rule"`

Only proceed past this section if the user wants to **run** reviews.

## Pre-flight — Verify Agent Availability

Before running reviews, check that the `deepwork:reviewer` agent is available. If it does not appear in the agents list (i.e., the Agent tool does not list `deepwork:reviewer` as a valid `subagent_type`), **STOP** and tell the user:

> The `deepwork:reviewer` agent is not available. Please run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the latest plugin updates, then try again.

Do not proceed with reviews until the agent is available.

## How to Run

1. Call the `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` tool directly:
   - **No arguments** to review the current branch's changes (auto-detects via git diff against the main branch).
   - **With `files`** to review only specific files: `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions(files=["src/app.py", "src/lib.py"])`. When provided, only reviews whose include/exclude patterns match the given files will be returned. Use this when the user asks to review a particular file or set of files rather than the whole branch.
   - **If the result says no rules are configured**: Ask the user if they'd like to auto-discover and set up rules. If yes, invoke the `/deepwork` skill with the `deepwork_reviews` job's `discover_rules` workflow. Stop here — do not proceed with running reviews if there are no rules.
2. The output will list review tasks to invoke in parallel. Each task has `description`, `subagent_type`, and `prompt` fields — these map directly to the Agent tool parameters. Launch all of them as parallel agents.
3. **While review agents run**, check for a changelog and open PR (see below).
4. Collect the results from all review agents.

## Changelog & PR Description Check

Run this concurrently with the review agents (step 2 above) — don't wait for reviews to finish first.

1. Check if the project has a changelog file (e.g., `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG`, `CHANGES.md`).
2. If a changelog exists and there are commits on the current branch beyond the main branch:
   - Read the changelog and the branch's commit log (`git log main..HEAD --oneline`).
   - Verify the changelog's unreleased/current section accurately reflects what the branch does. If entries are missing, outdated, or inaccurate, update the changelog.
3. If a PR is open for the current branch (check with `gh pr view`):
   - If you updated the changelog, also verify the PR description matches. Update it with `gh pr edit` if needed.
   - If the changelog was already accurate, skip the PR description check.

## Acting on Results

For each finding from the review agents:

- **Obviously good changes with no downsides** (e.g., fixing a typo, removing an unused import, adding a missing null check): make the change immediately without asking. When in doubt, ask.
- **Everything else** (refactors, style changes, architectural suggestions, anything with trade-offs):
  1. Use AskUserQuestion to ask the user about each finding **individually**. Do not group issues together unless they are the same issue occurring in multiple files; otherwise, use AskUserQuestion to ask about each issue separately. This lets the user make separate decisions on each item.
  2. For each question, provide several concrete fix approaches as options when there are reasonable alternatives (e.g., "Update the spec to match the code" vs "Update the code to match the spec" vs "Skip").
  3. If a finding seems minor or debatable, include an option to suppress that error in the future — such as a clarification to the rule if it is too narrow, or a comment on the offending content if comments work in that context.
  4. Be concise — quote the key finding, don't dump the full review.

When a finding is dismissed (user chooses "Skip" or you determine it's not actionable for this PR), call `mcp__deepwork__mark_review_as_passed` with the review's ID so it won't re-run on subsequent iterations.

## Iterate

After making any changes:

1. Call `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` with `files` set to **only the files you edited** during this iteration. This scopes the re-review to your changes rather than re-reviewing the entire branch.
2. Repeat the cycle (run → act on results → run again) until a clean run — one where all review agents return no findings, or all remaining findings have been explicitly skipped by the user.
3. On subsequent runs, you only need to re-run tasks that had findings last time — skip tasks that were clean.
4. Reviews that already passed are automatically skipped as long as reviewed files remain unchanged.

content.text:
I read the note, the source, the bench docs, and verified every external API claim against live docs. Findings below.

## Confirmed problems

**1. §4 / TL;DR row 3: "archy already ships the advisory/hard-fail contract" is overstated on three counts.**

Verified in `/Users/hosanglee/archy/src/archy/layers.py:52-54`:
```python
enabled: bool = False
tolerance: float = 0.0
mode: str = "error"
```

- **The dial is off by default and defaults to hard-fail when on.** `sdp.enabled` is `False`, so on a default archy install there is no advisory tier at all; and when enabled, `mode` defaults to `"error"`. The note never says this. A reader following §4's sentence "`sdp.mode: warn` in `archy.yaml` reports violations while leaving `passed` clean" would set only `mode` and get nothing, because `/Users/hosanglee/archy/src/archy/mcp.py:1122` gates the whole computation on `config.sdp.enabled`. Minimal correction: state that the dial requires `sdp.enabled: true` and that `mode` defaults to `error`.
- **SDP is not a "project rule".** The article's bullet is "which *project rules* are advisory and which are hard failures." The only thing with a dial is a built-in global heuristic (Stable Dependencies Principle). The rules a project actually authors (`forbid`) have no severity at all. So what ships is a *precedent* for the dial on one built-in check, not the contract the article asks for. The note's own "gap 1" is not a gap around the edge of a shipped feature, it is the feature. Minimal correction: demote the TL;DR/§4 headline from "archy already ships this contract" to "archy ships a working precedent for the dial (`sdp.mode`), scoped to one built-in heuristic that is off by default; project-authored `forbid` rules have no advisory tier, so the article's first bullet is a gap."
- **§4's first two bullets are in tension for `forbid`.** Bullet 1 says the dial is "owned by the project, not the runtime"; bullet 3 (block/feed-back/annotate "all derivable from one payload") is only true for `forbid` violations if the *guard* elects to ignore `passed`, i.e. the runtime owns the dial after all. content.text: Now the MCP protocol wording (finding 3), the §3 docs-recipe rationale (finding 4), and the `SPEC_VISUALIZATION` citation nit:

input.old_string: Worth naming the split, because it is the whole answer to question 2: **MCP gives the model the *option* to call archy; a guard runs archy whether the model wants to or not.** The article's fifth bullet ("a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed") is specifically the deterministic path. MCP by construction cannot express it: the protocol has no post-generation hook, only tools a model may elect to call.
input.new_string:
Worth naming the split precisely, because it is the whole answer to question 2, and the imprecise version of it is wrong.

**MCP has no mechanism for a server to intercept or gate the host agent's output.** Its server-initiated primitives (`sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create`, notifications) all run inside a server-handled operation and cannot be attached to the host's own loop. So the article's fifth bullet ("a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed") describes something the host must arrange; installing an MCP server does not arrange it.

What is *not* true, and what an earlier draft of this note asserted: that MCP calls are model-elected by construction. `tools/call` is issued by the client, not the model, so nothing stops a guard from deterministically invoking `archy_check` over the same MCP session instead of shelling out. The distinction is **who initiates the call**, not the protocol. That cuts in favor of the disposition below rather than against it: a guard can reuse an MCP session the runtime already holds, which shrinks the glue further and removes the last argument for a package to own it.

## 3. Question 2: MCP vs native adapters
**All four frameworks are already MCP clients.** `archy mcp` is reachable from every one of them today with zero archy code:

input.old_string: For the guard half, an adapter package would be: four packages, four release cadences, four dependency matrices, tracking four APIs that move fast (LangChain reworked its whole agent abstraction into the middleware model well inside the last year), in order to wrap a subprocess invocation and a JSON parse. The wrapped surface is trivially thin and the maintenance cost is not. **Native adapters fail the value test. Decided: no.**
input.new_string:
For the guard half, an adapter package would be: four packages, four release cadences, four dependency matrices, tracking four APIs that move fast (LangChain reworked its whole agent abstraction into the middleware model well inside the last year), in order to wrap a subprocess invocation and a JSON parse, or an MCP `tools/call` the runtime is already positioned to make. The wrapped surface is trivially thin and the maintenance cost is not. **Native adapters fail the value test. Decided: no.**

### What about a docs recipe instead?

The cheap version of "integration" is a page of copy-paste guards, one per framework. It is not free either: four untested snippets against four APIs that move at the rate §3 describes is a page that rots, and a rotted recipe is worse than no recipe because it carries archy's name. The version worth shipping is **one framework, tested in CI, kept current** rather than four snapshots. Pydantic AI is the pick if it ever happens: `output_validator` + `ModelRetry` is the closest semantic fit (feedback-and-retry rather than hard-stop-only), it is Python-native so the test runs in archy's existing suite, and pydantic is already a first-order dependency.

Even that is gated on §7, because a recipe is a distribution channel and there is nothing yet asking to be distributed to.

1	# Constraint-aware orchestration: should archy ship agent-framework integrations?
2	
3	Research answer to [#298]. Reads the DevDigest article [*Constraint Decay Is the Coding Agent Bug Nobody Can Prompt Around*][devdigest] (covering arXiv [2605.06445][paper]) for what its "What This Means for Agent Frameworks" section actually asks of a tool like archy, and asks whether archy should ship first-class integrations with LangChain/LangGraph, Pydantic AI, CrewAI, or the OpenAI Agents SDK.
4	
5	**Recommendation: no native adapters (wontfix), one tested docs recipe deferred behind a usage signal, and do not run the Q4 bench as specified.** Two small archy-side items fall out that stand on their own merit regardless of any framework.
6	
7	## TL;DR
8	
9	| Question (#298) | Answer |
10	| --- | --- |
11	| 1. Integration surfaces per framework | All four have a deterministic post-generation hook. Each maps to archy in 10 to 30 lines of glue. Nothing archy-specific has to exist. |
12	| 2. MCP vs native adapters | All four are already MCP clients, so `archy mcp` reaches them today with zero archy code. Adapters would wrap a subprocess call and a JSON parse across four fast-moving APIs. **Native adapters: no.** |
13	| 3. Hard-fail vs advisory semantics | **archy ships a working precedent for the dial, not the contract.** `sdp.mode: warn\|error` feeding `CheckPayload.passed` proves the mechanism out, but it is scoped to one built-in heuristic that is off by default; project-authored `forbid` rules have no advisory tier at all. So the article's first bullet is a real gap, and it is archy-side, not framework-side. |
14	| 4. Structural verifier as a gate (prototype + bench) | **Do not run as specified: the claim is close to tautological.** A gate that blocks until `archy check` passes produces artifacts that pass `archy check` by construction. Only a held-out-constraint design is non-trivial; recorded below, not scheduled. |
15	| 5. White paper tie-in | A short applications subsection, not a separate integration RFC. One paragraph plus one code block. |
16	| Usage-signal gate | **Zero inbound demand.** `ADOPTERS.md` is empty and every issue in the repo is maintainer-authored. This is entirely paper-motivated, which is the case the ticket's own second gate exists to catch. |
17	
18	## 1. What the article actually asks for
19	
20	The relevant passage lists five things an agent runtime should know:
21	
22	> - which project rules are advisory and which are hard failures
23	> - which files are exemplars for this task
24	> - which checks prove architecture, data, and security constraints
25	> - when to stop generating and ask for a design decision
26	> - when a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed
27	
28	Read carefully, four of the five are *properties of a project's configuration and its verifiers*, not properties of an agent framework. archy's `archy.yaml` plus `archy check` is already a worked example of bullets 1, 3, and 5 for the architecture dimension specifically. Bullet 2 (exemplars) is [#138]; bullet 4 (stop and ask) is a policy the runtime owner writes, not something a verifier can supply.
29	
30	So the article's ask decomposes into: *have a deterministic structural verifier with a machine-readable pass/fail and an advisory tier* (archy has this) and *call it from the loop* (the framework's job). The interesting question is only whether archy should ship the calling code.
31	
32	## 2. The integration surfaces, mapped
33	
34	Every one of the four frameworks has a deterministic hook that fires after generation, independent of what the model chose to do. This is the important property: it is where a verifier gate belongs.
35	
36	| Framework | Extension point | Failure semantics available |
37	| --- | --- | --- |
38	| **LangChain / LangGraph** | `create_agent(middleware=[...])` with an `after_model` hook (or, in raw LangGraph, a plain node plus a conditional edge) | Full control: the middleware can mutate state, inject a message, or `jump_to` another node. Retry, block, and annotate are all expressible. |
39	| **Pydantic AI** | `@agent.output_validator` | `raise ModelRetry("...")` feeds the message back to the model and consumes one unit of the output retry budget (default 1, settable via `Agent(retries={'output': N})`). Returning normally passes. Closest fit to "inject feedback and retry". |
40	| **CrewAI** | `Task(guardrails=[fn], guardrail_max_retries=N)` | `fn(TaskOutput) -> (bool, Any)`; on `(False, "message")` the string becomes the retry feedback, bounded by `guardrail_max_retries`. Same shape as Pydantic AI. |
41	| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | `@output_guardrail` returning `GuardrailFunctionOutput(tripwire_triggered=True)` | Hard stop only: raises `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` and halts the run. There is no built-in feedback-and-retry path; the caller builds the loop around the exception. |
42	
43	The glue in each case is: run `archy check` (or `archy diff` against a pre-edit snapshot), read `passed`, and on failure format the violations into a message. That is 10 to 30 lines. Nothing in it is hard, and nothing in it needs to live in archy.
44	
45	Worth naming the split precisely, because it is the whole answer to question 2, and the imprecise version of it is wrong.
46	
47	**MCP has no mechanism for a server to intercept or gate the host agent's output.** Its server-initiated primitives (`sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create`, notifications) all run inside a server-handled operation and cannot be attached to the host's own loop. So the article's fifth bullet ("a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed") describes something the host must arrange; installing an MCP server does not arrange it.
48	
49	What is *not* true, and what an earlier draft of this note asserted: that MCP calls are model-elected by construction. `tools/call` is issued by the client, not the model, so nothing stops a guard from deterministically invoking `archy_check` over the same MCP session instead of shelling out. The distinction is **who initiates the call**, not the protocol. That cuts in favor of the disposition below rather than against it: a guard can reuse an MCP session the runtime already holds, which shrinks the glue further and removes the last argument for a package to own it.
50	
51	## 3. Question 2: MCP vs native adapters
52	
53	**All four frameworks are already MCP clients.** `archy mcp` is reachable from every one of them today with zero archy code:
54	
55	- LangChain/LangGraph: `langchain-mcp-adapters`, `MultiServerMCPClient(...).get_tools()`
56	- Pydantic AI: `MCPToolset('...')` passed as a toolset (stdio path, local script, or Streamable HTTP)
57	- CrewAI: the `mcps=[...]` field on `Agent`, or `MCPServerAdapter` from `crewai-tools[mcp]`
58	- OpenAI Agents SDK: `MCPServerStdio` / `MCPServerStreamableHttp`, or `HostedMCPTool` with per-tool approval callbacks
59	
60	So the tool-access half of "integration" is already done and has been for as long as those adapters have existed. A native `archy-langgraph` package would add nothing there.
61	
62	For the guard half, an adapter package would be: four packages, four release cadences, four dependency matrices, tracking four APIs that move fast (LangChain reworked its whole agent abstraction into the middleware model well inside the last year), in order to wrap a subprocess invocation and a JSON parse, or an MCP `tools/call` the runtime is already positioned to make. The wrapped surface is trivially thin and the maintenance cost is not. **Native adapters fail the value test. Decided: no.**
63

## 5. Question 4: the gate bench, and why not to run it as specified

The ticket proposes prototyping an agent loop that runs `archy check` / `archy diff` as a post-generation gate, retries on structural failure, and measures whether that reduces constraint decay on a toy backend task.

**The claim as stated cannot fail in an interesting way.** If the loop blocks until `archy check` passes, then the final artifact passes `archy check` by construction. Measuring "the gate enforced the thing the gate checks" is theater by the definition archy already uses. This is precisely the failure mode the [#289]/[#294] arm-C work was built to avoid, and that line cost a full harness plus 44 live agent runs to return a documented null and a NO-GO on `archy brief`. Repeating that spend on a claim with a guaranteed positive is worse, not better.

**The obvious endpoint is tautological, but only that endpoint, and only under unbounded retry.** If the loop blocks until `archy check` passes, the final artifact passes `archy check` by construction, and measuring "the gate enforced the thing the gate checks" is theater by the definition archy already uses. That is the trap the [#289]/[#294] arm-C work was built to avoid, at a cost of a full harness plus 44 live agent runs for a documented null and a NO-GO on `archy brief`.

It would overstate the case to stop there, so: every retry mechanism in §2 is **bounded** (Pydantic AI's output budget defaults to 1, CrewAI has `guardrail_max_retries`, a LangChain `jump_to` loop needs a cap). Under a bounded budget the terminal artifact is not guaranteed to pass, and at least three endpoints have a real possible null:

- **Retries-to-green / fix-rate within budget.** Handed archy's violation text, does the model repair the layer violation or thrash? This is the sharpest of the three, because it measures whether archy's findings are *model-actionable*, which is the premise §4 gap 2 rests on.
- **Cost of the gate.** Added tokens and wall-clock per run. Plainly non-tautological, and the #259 harness already records both.
- **Collateral quality under structural pressure.** Does the agent satisfy `archy check` by gaming it (deleting the import, inserting a pass-through indirection) and regress the suite? `bench/agent_footprint_results.md` already tracks regressions as a first-class metric.

**The disposition is unchanged, but it rests on cost and §7, not on tautology.** None of the three has a feature riding on the answer today, all of them need the live-agent harness and enough N for a sign test, and the usage signal is zero. Recorded here so a future revisit starts from the right endpoints rather than the obvious wrong one. Of the three, retries-to-green is the one to run first if §4 gap 2 is ever built and its value questioned.

# Research

Curated, published research behind archy's design decisions: the literature survey and the empirical studies that gate which metrics ship, get deferred, or get rejected. These are the version-controlled, citable counterparts to raw working notes; they are referenced from the [README](../../README.md), [`ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md), and [`FUTURE.md`](../FUTURE.md).

| Doc | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`RESEARCH_METRICS.md`](RESEARCH_METRICS.md) | The literature survey: ~15 architecture-quality metrics evaluated for Python-specific applicability, plus the AI-agent-feedback section (§14) tying archy to the 2025-2026 coding-agent research (Navigation Paradox, LocAgent, Constraint Decay). The catalogue that informs the roadmap. |
| [`AXIS_REVIEW.md`](AXIS_REVIEW.md) | The OECD composite-indicator framework applied to every score-axis-promotion decision (why 5 axes, why `calls_per_edge` is not a 6th). |
| [`CALL_WEIGHTED_Q_EMPIRICS.md`](CALL_WEIGHTED_Q_EMPIRICS.md) | Empirical study behind v0.21's call-weighted Newman Q diagnostic (why it ships as a parallel diagnostic, not an axis replacement). |
| [`DSM_EMPIRICS.md`](DSM_EMPIRICS.md) | Why `archy dsm` ships as visualization-only and no DSM-derived scalar becomes a score axis or diagnostic. |
| [`SCORE_SHAPE_REDESIGN_EMPIRICS.md`](SCORE_SHAPE_REDESIGN_EMPIRICS.md) | The 28-project study of acyclicity/depth reformulations and aggregator alternatives that concluded against any axis change. |
| [`ACYCLICITY_DILUTION_EMPIRICS.md`](ACYCLICITY_DILUTION_EMPIRICS.md) | The #192 decision: should `overall` be changed so a single cycle registers at scale? Corpus study of count-sensitive acyclicity terms; rejected (they penalize large near-acyclic codebases and duplicate the FP-free `cycles.added` signal). The dilution is documented as intended. Harness in `bench/acyclicity_dilution.py`. |
| [`TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md`](TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md) | The study that rejected type-hint coverage in both axis and diagnostic form. |
| [`AUTONOMY_CONTINUUM_SYNTHESIS.md`](AUTONOMY_CONTINUUM_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Tracy Bannon's AI Autonomy Continuum talk: where archy sits on the continuum, the productivity-theater / score-gaming risk, and autonomy-tiered gating (deterministic checks may block, inferential checks stay advisory). Positioning and vocabulary, not new metrics. |
| [`AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md`](AGENT_CAUSAL_REASONING_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Phroneses' "Agents Cannot Maintain Systems" (additive vs transformative gap), tested against the 2025-2026 causal-reasoning, fitness-function, and AI-PR-review literature. Frames archy as an externalized causal model; maps the article's five causal dimensions to archy's surface (gap analysis); proposes `archy_simulate` (counterfactual pre-edit check) for agent causal reasoning and a per-PR structural review brief for human judgment. Positioning and design input, not new metrics. |
| [`PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md`](PREWALK_READ_REDUCTION_SYNTHESIS.md) | Synthesis of Stencil's "Prewalk" (the agent bill is `O(reads)`, not `O(edits)`) against archy's big question (#289): can an archy structural pre-edit brief reduce the exploratory reads an agent does before editing? Concludes prewalk's warm-trajectory handoff is not something a tool-mediated artifact can replicate (archy is weak for the handoff analogue), leaving only the substitution claim, which archy already half-ships (`invariant_brief`, `impact`, `graph(focus)`) but had never been measured. **Outcome: a documented non-result.** The #259 harness's arm-C extension ran to N=22 (`claude-sonnet-5`, flask); the brief did not reliably reduce reads-before-first-edit (pre_edit_reads median Δ −2.0, 14/8 pairs, sign p=0.286, after an N=10 hint at p=0.109 that did not survive more data). **NO-GO on any `archy brief` surface, now on evidence**, not an unproven prior (see `bench/agent_footprint_results.md`). |
| [`CONSTRAINT_AWARE_ORCHESTRATION_SYNTHESIS.md`](CONSTRAINT_AWARE_ORCHESTRATION_SYNTHESIS.md) | Answer to #298: should archy ship agent-framework integrations (LangGraph, Pydantic AI, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK) to serve the DevDigest/Constraint-Decay call for "constraint-aware orchestration"? Finding: the capability the article asks for is **already shipped** (`sdp.mode: warn\|error` feeding `CheckPayload.passed` is the advisory-vs-hard-failure dial), all four frameworks are already MCP clients, and the remaining guard glue is 10-30 lines per framework. **Native adapters wontfix; docs recipe deferred behind a usage signal (zero inbound demand today); the proposed gate bench rejected as tautological** (a gate that blocks until `archy check` passes yields passing artifacts by construction), with the only non-trivial design (held-out constraints) recorded but not scheduled. Two independently-justified archy-side gaps fall out: per-rule severity, and a canned remediation string. |
| [`INLOOP_PREVALENCE_EMPIRICS.md`](INLOOP_PREVALENCE_EMPIRICS.md) | Empirical answer to the synthesis's deepest open question. Replays 1,072 human-authored commits across 11 mature repos to measure how often a real change introduces a structural regression archy catches. Finding: new import cycles are rare per commit (0.5%) but concentrate in large changes (median 7x the files) and are severe when they fire; the composite score drops on 29% of commits but 98% of drops are sub-0.005 noise (validating the advisory-vs-blocking split). Reframes archy as a rare-firing, low-FP gate; specifies the agent A/B protocol for the remaining causal question. Harness in `bench/inloop_prevalence.py`. |

For *why we built what we built* (retrospective design rationale and competitive positioning), see [`../LEARNINGS.md`](../LEARNINGS.md). For the forward roadmap, see [`../ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md) and [`../FUTURE.md`](../FUTURE.md).

1	# Constraint-aware orchestration: should archy ship agent-framework integrations?
2	
3	Research answer to [#298]. Reads the DevDigest article [*Constraint Decay Is the Coding Agent Bug Nobody Can Prompt Around*][devdigest] (covering arXiv [2605.06445][paper]) for what its "What This Means for Agent Frameworks" section actually asks of a tool like archy, and asks whether archy should ship first-class integrations with LangChain/LangGraph, Pydantic AI, CrewAI, or the OpenAI Agents SDK.
4	
5	**Recommendation: no native adapters (wontfix), one tested docs recipe deferred behind a usage signal, and the Q4 bench not scheduled.** The finding that drives it: the half of the article's ask that archy does not already satisfy is an **archy config gap**, not an integration gap, so two small archy-side items fall out that stand on their own merit regardless of any framework.
6	
7	## TL;DR
8	
9	| Question (#298) | Answer |
10	| --- | --- |
11	| 1. Integration surfaces per framework | All four have a deterministic post-generation hook. Each maps to archy in 10 to 30 lines of glue. Nothing archy-specific has to exist. |
12	| 2. MCP vs native adapters | All four are already MCP clients, so `archy mcp` reaches them today with zero archy code. Adapters would wrap a subprocess call and a JSON parse across four fast-moving APIs. **Native adapters: no.** |
13	| 3. Hard-fail vs advisory semantics | **archy ships a working precedent for the dial, not the contract.** `sdp.mode: warn\|error` feeding `CheckPayload.passed` proves the mechanism out, but it is scoped to one built-in heuristic that is off by default; project-authored `forbid` rules have no advisory tier at all. So the article's first bullet is a real gap, and it is archy-side, not framework-side. |
14	| 4. Structural verifier as a gate (prototype + bench) | **Not scheduled, on cost and zero usage signal.** Its pass-rate endpoint is tautological (a gate that blocks until `archy check` passes yields passing artifacts by construction), but three bounded-retry endpoints are not: retries-to-green, gate cost, collateral regressions. Plus a held-out-constraint design that tests generalization. All recorded, none scheduled. |
15	| 5. White paper tie-in | A short applications subsection, not a separate integration RFC. One paragraph plus one code block. |
16	| Usage-signal gate | **Zero inbound demand.** `ADOPTERS.md` is empty and every issue in the repo is maintainer-authored. This is entirely paper-motivated, which is the case the ticket's own second gate exists to catch. |
17	
18	## 1. What the article actually asks for
19	
20	The relevant passage lists five things an agent runtime should know:
21	
22	> - which project rules are advisory and which are hard failures
23	> - which files are exemplars for this task
24	> - which checks prove architecture, data, and security constraints
25	> - when to stop generating and ask for a design decision
26	> - when a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed
27	
28	Read carefully, four of the five are *properties of a project's configuration and its verifiers*, not properties of an agent framework. archy's `archy.yaml` plus `archy check` is a worked example of bullets 3 and 5 for the architecture dimension specifically, and a partial one of bullet 1 (see §4). Bullet 2 (exemplars) is [#138]; bullet 4 (stop and ask) is a policy the runtime owner writes, not something a verifier can supply.
29	
30	So the article's ask decomposes into: *have a deterministic structural verifier with a machine-readable pass/fail and an advisory tier* and *call it from the loop* (the framework's job). archy has the verifier and the pass/fail; the advisory tier turns out to be only half-built (§4). The interesting question is whether archy should ship the calling code, and the answer is entangled with the fact that the missing half is on archy's side of the line, not the framework's.
31	
32	## 2. The integration surfaces, mapped
33	
34	Every one of the four frameworks has a deterministic hook that fires after generation, independent of what the model chose to do. This is the important property: it is where a verifier gate belongs.
35	
36	| Framework | Extension point | Failure semantics available |
37	| --- | --- | --- |
38	| **LangChain / LangGraph** | `create_agent(middleware=[...])` with an `after_model` hook (or, in raw LangGraph, a plain node plus a conditional edge) | Full control: the middleware can mutate state, inject a message, or `jump_to` another node. Retry, block, and annotate are all expressible. |
39	| **Pydantic AI** | `@agent.output_validator` | `raise ModelRetry("...")` feeds the message back to the model and consumes one unit of the output retry budget (default 1, settable via `Agent(retries={'output': N})`). Returning normally passes. Closest fit to "inject feedback and retry". |
40	| **CrewAI** | `Task(guardrails=[fn], guardrail_max_retries=N)` | `fn(TaskOutput) -> (bool, Any)`; on `(False, "message")` the string becomes the retry feedback, bounded by `guardrail_max_retries`. Same shape as Pydantic AI. |
41	| **OpenAI Agents SDK** | `@output_guardrail` returning `GuardrailFunctionOutput(tripwire_triggered=True)` | Hard stop only: raises `OutputGuardrailTripwireTriggered` and halts the run. There is no built-in feedback-and-retry path; the caller builds the loop around the exception. |
42	
43	The glue in each case is: run `archy check` (or `archy diff` against a pre-edit snapshot), read `passed`, and on failure format the violations into a message. That is 10 to 30 lines. Nothing in it is hard, and nothing in it needs to live in archy.
44	
45	Worth naming the split precisely before §3 takes up question 2, because the imprecise version of it is wrong.
46	
47	**MCP has no mechanism for a server to intercept or gate the host agent's output.** Its server-initiated primitives (`sampling/createMessage`, `elicitation/create`, notifications) all run inside a server-handled operation and cannot be attached to the host's own loop. So the article's fifth bullet ("a passing test suite is insufficient because the structural verifier failed") describes something the host must arrange; installing an MCP server does not arrange it.
48	
49	What is *not* true, and what an earlier draft of this note asserted: that MCP calls are model-elected by construction. `tools/call` is issued by the client, not the model, so nothing stops a guard from deterministically invoking `archy_check` over the same MCP session instead of shelling out. The distinction is **who initiates the call**, not the protocol. That cuts in favor of the disposition below rather than against it: a guard can reuse an MCP session the runtime already holds, which shrinks the glue further and removes the last argument for a package to own it.
50	
51	## 3. Question 2: MCP vs native adapters
52	
53	**All four frameworks are already MCP clients.** `archy mcp` is reachable from every one of them today with zero archy code:
54	
55	- LangChain/LangGraph: `langchain-mcp-adapters`, `MultiServerMCPClient(...).get_tools()`
56	- Pydantic AI: `MCPToolset('...')` passed as a toolset (stdio path, local script, or Streamable HTTP)
57	- CrewAI: the `mcps=[...]` field on `Agent`, or `MCPServerAdapter` from `crewai-tools[mcp]`
58	- OpenAI Agents SDK: `MCPServerStdio` / `MCPServerStreamableHttp`, or `HostedMCPTool` with per-tool approval callbacks
59	
60	So the tool-access half of "integration" is already done and has been for as long as those adapters have existed. A native `archy-langgraph` package would add nothing there.
61	
62	For the guard half, an adapter package would be: four packages, four release cadences, four dependency matrices, tracking four APIs that move fast (LangChain reworked its whole agent abstraction into the middleware model well inside the last year), in order to wrap a subprocess invocation and a JSON parse, or an MCP `tools/call` the runtime is already positioned to make. The wrapped surface is trivially thin and the maintenance cost is not. **Native adapters fail the value test. Decided: no.**
63	
64	### What about a docs recipe instead?
65

Everything is done and consistent across the doc, the PR, the issue, and memory.

**Review outcome.** The two configured `.deepreview` rules (no-em-dashes, doc-drift) passed clean on both runs. The adversarial pass earned its keep: it refuted three load-bearing claims, and I verified the biggest one myself against `layers.py:53-55` before acting.

The one that mattered: **"archy already ships the advisory/hard-fail contract" was wrong.** `SdpConfig.enabled` defaults to `False` and `mode` defaults to `"error"`, with `mcp.py:1122` gating the whole SDP computation on `enabled`, so `sdp.mode: warn` alone does nothing and a default install has no advisory tier. And SDP is a built-in heuristic, not a project rule, while `forbid` (what users actually write) has no severity at all. So the article's first bullet is a genuine gap. It doesn't revive the integration case, since an integration wouldn't close it either, but it does promote **#309 from a nicety to the item that would actually make that bullet true of archy** (I updated the ticket's framing in the note and memory accordingly).

The other two: my tautology argument only covered the pass-rate endpoint under *unbounded* retry, and every framework budget is bounded (Pydantic AI defaults to 1), so retries-to-green, gate cost, and collateral regressions are all real measurables. The bench stays unscheduled, now on cost and the zero usage signal. And "MCP gives the model the option to call archy" was wrong as a protocol claim: `tools/call` is client-issued. The narrowed version (MCP can't gate the *host's* output) is true and strengthens the no-adapters call.

A verification agent then caught six residual inconsistencies from my own edits, including an off-by-one on the `layers.py` citation I had just added. All fixed.

**Landed:** PR [#311](https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/pull/311) (two commits, draft plus corrections, body rewritten), a [correction comment](https://github.com/hslee16/Archy/issues/298#issuecomment-5075749504) on #298 since my first comment carried the overstatement, and #309/#310 filed.

Two notes: `gh pr edit` and `gh issue view` both fail in this repo with a Projects-classic deprecation error, so I used the REST API for the body update. And there's no changelog file, so nothing to sync there.
